results.summary: This is an interactive Morse code learning game that displays letters on a 7-segment display and requires the user to input the correct Morse pattern via a switch. It provides immediate feedback and progresses through the English alphabet. The design can be tested in simulation or on hardware. It is implemented in Verilog and runs on a 100 Hz clock.

This project is a gate test design that allows users to experiment with different logic gates by toggling switches and observing the outputs. It is implemented in Wokwi and uses interconnected gates between inputs and outputs. External hardware includes switches and a single number LED display. The design is intended for educational testing of logic gate behavior.

This design generates a bouncing ROOTS logo with a kaleidoscope background for VGA output. It is intended to be connected to a VGA monitor via a Tiny VGA Pmod. The design runs on a 25.175 MHz clock and occupies 2x2 tiles. It is a visual demo project.

This is a variable-length LFSR generator supporting 2-tap and 4-tap configurations with hold and step controls. It produces a new LFSR value each clock cycle, with the low-order 15 bits exposed on outputs. The design includes a valid signal to indicate a valid LFSR configuration. It was tested using hand-generated top-level test modules with simulation tools.

This is a RISC-V SoC with a GPU that performs vertex shading, rasterization, and RGB fragment shading. It renders a 10-frame animation of a rotating RGB triangle entirely in firmware, with no host-side rendering. The design uses a QSPI flash/PSRAM interface and can be tested on an FPGA with a pico-ice board and Raspberry Pi Debug Probe. It is implemented in Chisel and occupies 4x2 tiles.

This chip is a character-level language model that generates Shakespeare-like text using a ternary-weight transformer with all weights baked into ROM. It streams int16 residuals in and int8 residuals out, one token per transaction. The chip requires a host microcontroller (e.g., RP2350B) to handle text encoding and decoding, and it communicates via a byte protocol. The design includes a clock sweep test and a no-firmware test for bring-up.

This is a simplified 6502 processor that implements a subset of the original instruction set. It is built around an ALU, registers, and a microcoded instruction decoder. The design runs on a 40 MHz clock and occupies 1x2 tiles. It includes detailed documentation on verification approaches.

This is a Morse code generator circuit for the letters J and R. It uses a 4-bit synchronous counter and logic gates to simulate the dot and dash patterns. The design can be tested by connecting a 7-segment display and using a button to select the letter. It is a simple educational project.

This is a small RISC-V processor supporting the base RV32E instruction set plus Zicond and Zbs extensions. It uses two SPI memories: one read-only and one read-write, both with 2-byte addresses. The processor can be tested with a provided program that records GPIO inputs and outputs them after a delay. It requires external SPI flash and RAM, and runs on a 40 Hz clock.

This is a random number generator that exploits the unstable state of a latch when both S and R are set to 0. It includes many instances (34 per output pin) to maximize the chance of getting a working random source. The design has a freeze input to hold the outputs, and other inputs can wire outputs to other instances. The author notes that it may not work due to potential bias or constant outputs.
